title: 17 Tracking Studies: The Pandemic Did Not Ruin Child Development
dek: Follow the same children over time and the pandemic produced only mild declines or stagnation, followed by recovery; blaming today's attention problems in kids entirely on the pandemic lacks evidence.
why: Medium information density, but the conclusion is counterintuitive: cross-sectional comparisons amplified "learning loss," while longitudinal tracking shows developmental resilience. Suited to anyone who needs judgment about education narratives.
who: Parents, teachers and policy researchers focused on child development and education policy; and general readers who want to understand how "pandemic narratives" get amplified by the media.
skip: The ad segments at the start and in the middle can be skipped without affecting the core content.

points.body: The NAEP data the mass media often cites compares a different group of fourth graders in 2019 with a different group in 2022 — the former never experienced the pandemic, the latter went through cumulative disruption. This kind of cross-cohort comparison naturally magnifies the gap. This special issue required all studies to track the same children: the same group before, during and after the pandemic. Once within-individual differences are controlled for, the pattern in academic skills is far milder, and signs of recovery appear — after children returned to in-person school, reading and math returned to or even exceeded pre-pandemic levels.

points.h: One third of parents say the pandemic's impact was neutral to positive
points.body: Based on parents' self-reports, the pandemic was not a universal catastrophe. Across different studies, about one third of parents considered COVID's impact on their lives neutral or even positive, including low-income families — and the narrative that low-income families were utterly devastated by the pandemic does not hold up. Parents are their children's buffer; if parents themselves did not feel it was that bad, their children's experience at home was not that bad either. This finding was replicated across multiple studies and may be one reason academic and mental health outcomes did not turn catastrophic.

points.h: Kids with existing substance-use trajectories were pushed deeper
points.body: The most consistent finding among risk factors: risk that existed before the pandemic predicted worse outcomes after it. A sample from a middle- to high-income US community showed that adolescent substance use frequency during the pandemic was higher than before it, especially among kids who were already frequent users, and was exacerbated by factors such as household financial risk. This runs counter to the popular observation that "kids were stuck at home so substance use declined." But this is one of the few examples where a negative pattern was deepened; the larger theme remains that early risk predicts later risk — which has nothing to do with the pandemic and is an old conclusion of risk-and-resilience theory in developmental psychology.

points.h: Parent-child closeness did not drop — it became a protective factor
points.body: Adolescence is usually accompanied by declining parent-child closeness and rising depressive symptoms. But a sample from mainland China found that during the pandemic parent-child closeness did not show this decline, possibly because social isolation shrank the community down to just the family. Adolescents' depressive symptoms rose during the acute phase, then fell back and recovered, with no cumulative increase. Parent-child closeness may have acted as a buffer. This is consistent with George Bonanno's research: even with fluctuations, people return to baseline — just as the happiness of lottery winners fades within a few months.

points.h: Reading runs on daily conversation; math is harder to teach at home
points.body: Reading and language development are socially mediated, and in early years happen largely in conversation. During the worst phase of the pandemic, conversation in the home continued, so school closures hit reading less than math. Math needs more structure and practice, and parents are more anxious about teaching math. Hence reading recovered faster, math more slowly, and math recovery depended more on socioeconomic status — the Ghana sample showed better math recovery in higher-income, better-resourced environments. But neither the math nor the reading pandemic effect is enough to explain the long-term decline in US test scores; that trend began before the pandemic.

One study measured infants using DNA methylation clocks: before the pandemic, during it, and 30 months after the acute phase, and found no trace of biological aging. In other words, the pandemic left no wear at the biological level in infants. This directly rebuts the claim that "today's kindergarten and first-grade kids can't sit still because they're pandemic babies" — the inability to sit still may be real, but the cause is very likely not the pandemic, at least this study shows the pandemic did not even affect biological mechanisms.

points.h: Grade inflation hides real needs for support
points.body: An underrated mechanism: grades are inflating, test scores are falling or flat, and parents care more about the marks on a report card than about standardized tests. Tests are supposed to be diagnostic tools; districts usually have fall, mid-year and spring formative assessments to guide instruction. But if the report card looks good, many parents stop looking further. A child may actually need extra tutoring or support, yet no one knows test scores are falling, so no help comes, and the problem only surfaces in later performance.

points.h: Parent-teacher conferences should put the data on the table
points.body: One concrete, actionable suggestion: restructure parent-teacher conferences. Almost every school has them, but they usually are not organized around data. Johnson's proposal is — bring out the data, look at it together with parents, and ask them what questions they have. Of course some parents will say the child had just come back from a trip and hadn't slept well on test day, which is not accurate; but on average the data contains very useful information. Parents are their children's advocates and need to actively ask to see the information and have a collaborative, partner-like conversation with the teacher. Behind this is a bigger problem: over the past 15 years the relationship between parents and teachers has grown increasingly adversarial, and teachers may be afraid to raise a child's problems for fear of being attacked by parents.

terms.def: Research that tracks the same group of people over time, as distinct from cross-sectional comparisons of different cohorts.
The US National Assessment of Educational Progress, a standardized test given to fourth and eighth graders every two years, often cited as evidence of learning loss.
Measures that estimate biological age from DNA methylation levels, used to gauge physiological wear.
Cognitive abilities such as attention, persistence and inhibitory control, related to classroom performance.
Internalizing refers to inward-facing problems such as worry and sadness; externalizing refers to outward-facing problems such as aggression and rule-breaking.
